prime.problem: Attention scores are dot products, and a dot product doesn't know where a word sits. Without a position signal, the last word of the cat sat and of cat the sat sees exactly the same thing, so the model can't use word order.
prime.fits: Comes straight after the embedding lookup (\(x_0 = E[\ids]\)). It is the last thing added before attention, and it sets up the next cards: the scores \(QK^\top\) are where RoPE does its work.
expect: RoPE: turning each \(q\) and \(k\) pair by position × angle
prime.goal: Add a position row by hand, rotate a query and key pair and get 0.9101, and explain why the rotated score depends only on the distance between two words.

attend: Why does the last word's prediction not change when you swap the first two words of a model with no positions?
With a learned table, what is the only thing that makes the at position 2 different from the at position 0?
In the rotated dot product, which step makes the absolute positions cancel and leave only \(n - m\)?
Why does RoPE act on \(Q\) and \(K\) inside every layer, instead of once on the embeddings?
What goes wrong with a single rotating pair at large distances, and how do 32 pairs at different speeds fix it?

must: Attention compares words only through \(q \cdot k\) dot products → a dot product ignores where the vectors came from → with no position signal, swapping earlier words leaves the last word's output unchanged (measured: equal to 1.1e-16) → the model needs position injected somewhere

Learned positions: \(x_0[t] = E[\mathit{id}_t] + P[t]\) → the same word gets a different vector at each spot → \(P\) is trained by gradient like \(E\) (\(dP = dx_0\)) → but each position is a separate row, so the model can't go past the table's last row and learns position 3 and position 3,000 independently

RoPE turns each \(q\) pair by \(m\theta\) and each \(k\) pair by \(n\theta\) → rotations compose and \(R^\top\) undoes \(R\) → \(\big(R(m\theta)q\big)^\top\big(R(n\theta)k\big) = q^\top R\big((n-m)\theta\big)k\) → the score depends only on the distance: 0.9101 at (1,0), (3,2) and (7,6)

One pair is periodic (repeats every \(2\pi/\theta\) positions) → it can't tell some far distances from near ones → Qwen uses 32 pairs with \(\theta\) from 1 rad down to \(1.54 \times 10^{-6}\) rad per position → fast pairs resolve nearby words, slow pairs never wrap, and their scores add up in \(q \cdot k\)
elevated: RoPE goes on \(Q\) and \(K\) only, right before \(QK^\top\) → the angles cancel inside that dot product → \(V\) and the embeddings stay unrotated, so position changes which words are attended to, not what gets copied
A rotation keeps length (\(|k| = 1.0000\) before and after) → RoPE changes only directions → it adds no weights and doesn't blow up or shrink the scores
reference: \(\theta_i = b^{-2i/d}\); Qwen2.5 rope_theta = 1,000,000, head dim 64, 32 pairs, so \(\theta_i = 10^{6\cdot(-2i/64)}\)
pair 0: 1 rad/position (full turn every 6.3), pair 1: 0.649, pair 16: 0.001, pair 31: \(1.54 \times 10^{-6}\) (full turn every 4,080,185)
Hugging Face's Qwen/Llama code pairs number \(i\) with \(i + d/2\) (rotate_half) instead of neighbours; same math
GPT-2's \(P\) is \(1{,}024 \times 768\); the tiny model's \(P\) is \(3 \times 4\)

compress.prompt: Card closed: explain in 3–5 sentences why attention needs positions and the two ways to add them. Or draw two dials (\(q\) at 1, \(k\) at 0, and \(q\) at 3, \(k\) at 2) and use them to show why the score is the same.
checklist: dot products ignore order, so without positions the words are a bag
learned: add a trained row \(P[t]\) to each word's vector, once, at the bottom
RoPE: rotate each pair of \(q\) and \(k\) by position × angle, in every attention layer
the rotation angles subtract inside \(q \cdot k\), so only the distance \(n - m\) matters
many pairs at different speeds: fast for near words, slow for far ones

retrieve.q: Explain the difference between absolute and relative position, using the learned table and RoPE as the two examples.
answer: absolute: each position has its own learned row; the model sees where a word is
relative: RoPE's score depends only on how far apart query and key are
absolute rows are learned independently; the relative pattern works the same at every position

retrieve.q: Walk through computing the rotated score for one pair: \(q = [1,\ 0]\) at position 1, \(k = [0.6,\ 0.8]\) at position 0, \(\theta = 0.5\).
answer: \(k\) at position 0 turns by 0 and stays \([0.6,\ 0.8]\)

retrieve.q: You're designing a model that must read documents much longer than GPT-2's 1,024 tokens. Argue for RoPE over a learned position table, and say what it doesn't solve.
answer: a learned table has no row past its length, and each row costs \(d\) weights
RoPE has no table and no weights; any position just gets a bigger angle
but a model trained on short texts never saw slow pairs turn far, so going much longer still needs care (changing the angles)

retrieve.q: Why does the swap test in Try-this-first swap the first two words and look at the last prediction, instead of swapping any two words?
answer: with a causal mask, each word only sees itself and earlier words
the last word sees all three words either way, as the same set
if the last word moved, its own vector and what it can see would change, so the test would prove nothing

compare.q: The token table \(E\) and the position table \(P\) are both looked up and added. What does each one encode, what gives each one its gradient, and why can the model share \(E\)'s rows across positions but not \(P\)'s across words?
answer: \(E\): one row per word, the same at every position; \(P\): one row per position, the same for every word
both get their gradient from \(dx_0\): \(E\) only on the rows that were looked up, \(P\) on every row used
\(x_0[t] = E[\mathit{id}_t] + P[t]\) needs both, because neither alone says which word is where

compare.q: RoPE changes \(Q\) and \(K\) before \(QK^\top/\sqrt{d}\). Does rotating change the scale argument for dividing by \(\sqrt{d}\), and where exactly would the rotation slot into that card's equation?
answer: rotation keeps each pair's length, so the spread of \(q \cdot k\) doesn't grow: \(\sqrt{d}\) scaling is still right
the order is: \(Q = a\Wq\), \(K = a\Wk\), then rotate each row of \(Q\) and \(K\) by its position, then \(QK^\top/\sqrt{d}\) and the mask

predict.q: Suppose all three rows of the tiny model's \(P\) were set to the same vector. Would the model now tell the cat sat from cat the sat at the last position?
predict.answer: No. Adding the same vector to every word moves them all equally, so the last word still sees the same set of three vectors in either order. Its prediction is identical for both sentences (though not the same numbers as with no \(P\)). A position signal only helps if it is different at different positions.

apply.task: Without rotating anything, use the shortcut \(q \cdot k = 0.6\cos(0.5\,d) + 0.8\sin(0.5\,d)\) to get the score for a query at position 9 and a key at position 5 (\(\theta = 0.5\), \(q = [1,\ 0]\), \(k = [0.6,\ 0.8]\)). Then run llm-math/labs/positions-rope.py and find the matching line.
apply.done: You get 0.4777 (\(d = 4\): \(0.6 \cos 2 + 0.8 \sin 2 = -0.2497 + 0.7274\)), and it matches the lab's distance-4 line.
apply.hint: Only the distance matters: \(9 - 5 = 4\), so the angle is \(4 \times 0.5 = 2\) rad. \(\cos 2 = -0.4161\), \(\sin 2 = 0.9093\).

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: did you expect the swapped sentence to change the last prediction even without \(P\)?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why \(R(m\theta)^\top R(n\theta)\) becomes \(R\big((n - m)\theta\big)\), or why that leaves only the distance?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: rotation → angles subtract, or angles subtract → the same habit works at every position?
Could you explain to someone why Qwen needs 32 pairs and not just one?
What will you look for in the attention-scores card to see where rotated \(Q\) and \(K\) would plug in?
